title: Find Customer Referee
statement:
One table lists customers and who brought them in:

- `Customer(id, name, referee_id)`: one row per customer; `id` is unique. `referee_id` is the `id` of the customer who referred this one, or `null` when nobody did.

Report the `name` of every customer who was **not** referred by the customer with `id = 2`: that is, customers whose `referee_id` is a value other than 2, and customers with no referee at all (`null`). Output one column, `name`, with one row per qualifying customer (names may repeat). Rows may come in any order.
constraints: referee_id is null when the customer was not referred
Names are not unique; each qualifying customer gives its own row
reference:
SELECT c.name
FROM Customer AS c
WHERE c.referee_id IS NULL
   OR c.referee_id <> 2;
brute:
SELECT name
FROM Customer
WHERE id NOT IN (
  SELECT id
  FROM Customer
  WHERE referee_id = 2
)
notes:
## Intuition

The condition reads like a single comparison, `referee_id <> 2`, but SQL uses three-valued logic: comparing `null` with anything gives `unknown`, and `WHERE` keeps only rows whose condition is `true`. Customers with no referee would silently disappear, even though nobody (and so not customer 2) referred them. The fix is to accept the `null` case explicitly.

## Approach

1. Read every row of `Customer` (alias `c`).
2. Keep a row when `c.referee_id IS NULL` (nobody referred the customer) **or** `c.referee_id <> 2` (someone other than customer 2 did).
3. Select only `c.name`.

## Example 1, step by step

- Will, Jane and Bill have `referee_id = null`: the `IS NULL` test is true, so they are kept.
- Zack has `referee_id = 1`: `1 <> 2` is true, so he is kept.
- Alex and Mark have `referee_id = 2`: both tests are false, so they are dropped.

The result is Will, Jane, Bill and Zack.

## Complexity

- Time: O(N) for N customers; every row is checked once.
- Space: O(N) for the result in the worst case.

## Pitfalls

- `WHERE referee_id <> 2` (or `!= 2`) alone drops every customer whose `referee_id` is `null`.
- `WHERE NOT referee_id = 2` has the same problem: `NOT unknown` is still `unknown`.
- Adding `DISTINCT` merges different customers who share a name; each customer is its own row.

## Clauses

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `c` | `Customer`, the only table |
| `c.referee_id IS NULL` | customers nobody referred |
| `c.referee_id <> 2` | customers referred by someone other than customer 2 |

narration.1: Only the customer name is reported.
narration.2: Every customer row is a candidate.
narration.3: Keep customers with no referee: a null never equals 2, but a plain comparison would not say so.
narration.4: Also keep customers whose referee is someone other than customer 2.
